title: Weight, BMI and losing weight safely
question_forms: How do I lose weight or tone up safely?
What BMI is healthy for a Black person?
Does BMI work for muscular people?
tradition_says: Being bigger is often seen as healthy or attractive in many families, and weight comments are common. Lifters say BMI is useless.

layer1.plain_answer: The NHS says people from Black African or African-Caribbean backgrounds are at risk of health problems at a slightly lower BMI: 23 to 27.4 is overweight and 27.5 or more is obese. Lose weight steadily, about half to one kilogram a week, with a balanced diet and activity. BMI cannot tell muscle from fat.

do.text: Check your BMI against the lower cut-offs: 23 to 27.4 overweight, 27.5 or more obese for Black African or African-Caribbean adults.
Eat a balanced diet with plenty of fruit and vegetables and fewer high-fat or sugary foods.
Aim to lose weight steadily, about 0.5 to 1 kg a week.
Get active for 45 to 60 minutes a day if you are aiming to lose weight; shorter sessions count.
Cut down on alcohol, which is high in calories.

avoid.text: Fast weight loss: the UK's NHS advice is to lose weight steadily.
Relying on BMI alone if you carry a lot of muscle: it may put you in the overweight or obese category without much body fat.

see_someone_when: Your BMI is in the obese range for your background, or you have high blood pressure or type 2 diabetes with extra weight (doctor, for a weight-management plan).
You have gained weight quickly without a clear reason (doctor).

tested.population: 22,723 adults in the Health Surveys for England (1,379 African-Caribbean)
tested.design: Secondary analysis of cross-sectional surveys of blood pressure and BMI
tested.finding: African-Caribbean women had higher BMI than white women; there was little difference in BMI in men.

source.authors: Agyemang C, Humphry RW, Bhopal R

tested.note: Included only for the BMI pattern; this paper does not test the NHS BMI cut-offs.

tier_driver: That the lower BMI cut-offs fit Black African and African-Caribbean adults: NHS statement only; I opened no study that tests them.
tier_note: D because the claim is NHS guidance and my search for the evidence behind it found nothing in the pages I opened; the one B line is about BMI differences, not about cut-offs. Would move with the NICE evidence review.
harm_note: No harm signal found for steady weight loss. Rapid loss is advised against by the UK's NHS.
evidence_summary: The NHS uses lower BMI thresholds for adults from South Asian, Chinese, other Asian, Middle Eastern, Black African or African-Caribbean backgrounds: overweight from 23, obese from 27.5. Steady loss of about half to one kilogram a week, a balanced diet, less alcohol and activity are the NHS advice. The NHS also notes BMI cannot tell muscle from fat. I opened no study testing the cut-offs in Black adults.
measured_variables: BMI (weight divided by height squared); waist and body fat are alternatives not covered
Ethnic background, used by the NHS to set the cut-off; the underlying variable (body fat at a given BMI) was not shown in what I opened
gaps: Untested or not opened: NICE (UK) NG246 evidence for the ethnic-specific BMI cut-offs (the page I opened did not show them); body composition at equal BMI in Black adults; weight-loss medicines and surgery in Black adults (the UK's NHS gives lower BMI thresholds for surgery, 37.5, or 32.5 to 37.4 with a related condition, but I opened no study); muscle gain and "toning". The "get active 45 to 60 minutes" line is NHS weight-loss advice, not the general 150-minute target.

sources.authors: Agyemang C, Humphry RW, Bhopal R

elsewhere.text: In the US, NIDDK defines overweight as a BMI of 25 to 29.9 and obesity as 30 or above for adults.
elsewhere.page_date: date not clear; 'Last reviewed May 2023' shown

elsewhere.text: WHO defines adult overweight as a BMI of 25 or more and obesity as 30 or more.
